§6.10 Table of Contents

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

lists-table-of-contents · layout lists navigation

✅ Normative

A table of contents, table of authorities or index MUST be rendered as a list: one item per entry, nested as the page indents it, each item the label then its page number(s) exactly as printed, separated by a space. It MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

A contents page pairs each label with a page number, usually across a dot leader.

Chapter 3 — Reserving  . . . . . . . . . . . .  47
Chapter 4 — Pricing    . . . . . . . . . . . .  63

Rendering

Printed:   1  Introduction ....................  3
              1.1  Scope ......................  4
           2  Reserving .......................  47

- 1 Introduction 3
  - 1.1 Scope 4
- 2 Reserving 47
  • Every printed entry MUST survive, with its page number(s) attached to the right label.
  • The label and the number are separated by a single space. The dot leaders produce nothing — see Dot Leader Lines§6.1.
  • Nesting shown by indentation MUST be carried as list nesting, not flattened.
  • An entry with several page references keeps them all, as printed: HCR 2.603(A) 4-50, 4-57.
  • A contents page is navigation, not data: rendering it as a table would make it read as facts to anything that consumes the page. A list also holds a run of page references that a two-column table could only cram into one cell.

The exception is a contents page printed as a real ruled grid with column headers (Section | Title | Page). That is a table by the ordinary rules of Is This Even a Table§9.1.5, not a contents exception.

✅ Sample — a table of authorities with several pages per entry

HCR 2.603(D) 3-27, 4-49, 4-54, … — each rule followed by a run of page references in blue, no leaders, one to twelve references per line. A label paired with a list of numbers. The entries form a list, each rule followed by its references; the blue is decoration. The running header and footer bands open and close the page.
